passage:
Coach's note, Thursday evening badminton practice.
Ujjwal (second year) was off his game today. Between every set he went to his bag and checked his phone, then came back either grinning or flat. Kishore, his doubles partner, told me quietly that Ujjwal had asked a girl from his class, Pallavi, for coffee on Sunday after replying to her stories for two weeks, and she hadn't answered yet.
At the water break I heard Ujjwal say, "She replied in two minutes last time. Now it's been four hours. That means no, right?" He laughed as if joking, but he served into the net three times after that.
I told him to leave the phone in the bag till practice ended, and that four hours can simply mean someone is stuck in a lab. He nodded but didn't look convinced. I'll keep his drills light this week.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal ask Pallavi?
qa.a: Ujjwal asked Pallavi for coffee on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal afraid of as he checked his phone?
qa.a: Ujjwal was afraid Pallavi's slow reply meant rejection; the four-hour gap felt huge even though he laughed it off.

qa.q: How did the coach help at this stage, and what else might help Ujjwal?
qa.a: The coach suggested leaving the phone in the bag and pointed out other reasons for a slow reply; Ujjwal could also remind himself that one reply time is not an answer.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel watching Ujjwal this evening?
qa.a: Kishore probably feels a mix of sympathy and worry, sharing it quietly with the coach and seeing it affect their doubles game.

grounding: Shows a young man who has replied to a girl's stories and asked her for coffee, fearing rejection and treating reply speed as hugely important.

passage:
Tuesday, 1 a.m.
Replied to Riddhima's story about her rooftop plants with a sunflower. A sunflower? What was I thinking. She reacted with a laugh though. That's good? Or polite?
Finally asked if she wants to get coffee after the Friday lab. Typed it eleven times. Chinmay said "bro, just send it", grabbed my phone and pressed send before I could delete it again.
She replied: "sure, sounds fun!"
I've read that maybe forty times. "Sure" feels a bit flat. But then there's "sounds fun" with an exclamation mark. Does the exclamation mark cancel the "sure"? Chinmay says a grown man shouldn't analyse punctuation like it's a board exam.
He's right. I'm scared she's just being nice. But she said yes. She said YES.
Thomas

qa.q: How many times did Thomas type the coffee message?
qa.a: Thomas typed it eleven times.

qa.q: What is Thomas worried about when he rereads 'sure, sounds fun!'?
qa.a: Thomas is scared Riddhima is just being nice, so even the punctuation feels like a clue to whether she really wants to go.

qa.q: What could help Thomas before Friday's coffee?
qa.a: Thomas could take the yes at face value, stop decoding punctuation, and focus on enjoying an ordinary conversation with Riddhima. 😊

qa.q: How does Chinmay see Thomas's worry?
qa.a: Chinmay finds it a bit much, which is why he pressed send and joked about the board exam, but he is also nudging Thomas to be brave.

grounding: Illustrates a young man replying to a girl's stories, asking her for coffee and rereading her text, with fear of rejection under the play.

passage:
Okay, I'm Darshan, and I'll admit it. I watched Kiran's story from the hiking trip eleven times.

Not in a creepy way. I just wanted to find the right thing to reply. I typed "Wow!" and deleted it. Too boring. Typed "Next time take me!" and deleted it. Too much. Finally I sent a mountain emoji. Then I stared at my phone.

She replied in four minutes. Four. I screenshotted it and sent it to my roommate.

Two days later I asked her for coffee. I rehearsed it in the mirror, very casual: "If you're free sometime..." She took three hours to reply and I was convinced she hated me. Turns out she was in a lab.

The thing is, I act chill. I joke. But inside, every reply feels like a verdict.

qa.q: How many times did Darshan watch Kiran's story?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling during the three hours before Kiran replied?
qa.a: He felt anxious and afraid of rejection, convinced she hated him, because each small signal felt enormous.

qa.q: What could Darshan remind himself when a reply takes a long time?
qa.a: That a slow reply often has a simple reason, like being in a lab, and does not have to mean rejection.

qa.q: How might Kiran see the three-hour gap?
qa.a: To her it was just time in the lab, with no hidden message, so she likely had no idea he was worried.

grounding: Darshan replies to Kiran's story, asks her for coffee and reads her replies closely, hiding a fear of rejection that makes reply speed feel huge.

passage:
Friday. Tomás finally replied to Maria's photo of the sunset over the Lisbon river: "That's the best view in the city 🙂". He rewrote it five times before sending. She hearted it within a minute. He grinned at his screen for the rest of the bus ride.

Tuesday, four days later. He suggested coffee after their Portuguese literature seminar. She said, "Maybe Thursday?" He spent the whole evening decoding the "maybe". Was it polite? Was it a no?

Thursday. They met. It went well: she laughed at his joke about their professor. That night he texted, "Thanks for today." She didn't reply for six hours. He checked his phone every ten minutes, rereading his message and hating the full stop.

At midnight she wrote, "Sorry, family dinner! Loved it. Again soon?"

He read it four times. Then he let himself breathe.

qa.q: When did Tomás suggest coffee?
qa.a: After their Portuguese literature seminar.

qa.q: Why does Tomás keep checking his phone every ten minutes?
qa.a: He is anxious and afraid of rejection, reading the six-hour silence as a possible sign that she didn't enjoy it.

qa.q: What small step could help Tomás with the waiting?
qa.a: He could put the phone away for a while and remind himself that silence usually has an ordinary reason, like a family dinner.

qa.q: How does Maria probably see her six-hour delay?
qa.a: To her it was just a family dinner, and she replied warmly afterwards, not knowing how anxious it made him.

grounding: Over a week Tomás replies to Maria's stories, suggests coffee and rereads her texts, his fear of rejection making every reply delay feel huge.

passage:
Nikita, you want to know how I got your Ira mami to go out with me? Your Mama will tell you, but you have to promise not to laugh.

I was twenty, she was in my accounting class. I replied to every post she put up on the college page. A comment on her rangoli, a comment on her debate prize. I thought I was being subtle.

When I finally asked her for tea at the stall near the gate, I wrote the message on paper first. Changed three words. Sent it.

She took a whole afternoon to reply. I sat in the library pretending to study and felt sick. I was sure she'd say no and tell her friends.

She said yes. Later she told me she'd been at her cousin's wedding all day.

The turning point, Nikita, was sending that message at all. Fear nearly stopped me.

qa.q: Where did Mama ask Ira to have tea?
qa.a: At the stall near the gate.

qa.q: What does Mama's feeling sick in the library show about his state of mind?
qa.a: It shows he was afraid of rejection and anxious that a slow reply meant a no.

qa.q: What choice in the story mattered most?
qa.a: Sending the message at all despite his fear; if he had let fear stop him, nothing would have started.

qa.q: How might Ira have felt coming back from the wedding to his message?
qa.a: She may have been pleasantly surprised and pleased, with no idea he had been so anxious.

grounding: Mama recalls replying to Ira's posts, asking her for tea and dreading her slow reply, showing the fear of rejection beneath a young man's approach.

passage: The hostel lights died at nine, and Abhay's phone showed six percent. Of course it did. An hour earlier, after deleting it three times, he had finally sent Nandini: "There's a new chai place near the library. Saturday?" Before that he had only replied to her stories, a clapping reaction on her sketch, a "haha" on her burnt noodles. Now the word Seen sat under his message and nothing else. He dimmed the screen to save battery and kept waking it anyway. Four minutes. Eleven. Last time she had answered in two minutes; did the gap mean something? His roommate snored. At five percent the phone buzzed: "Saturday works! Can we make it 5? I have lab till 4 😊" Abhay read it five times by torchlight, grinning in the dark, and did not dare use the last of the battery to reply properly.

qa.q: How much battery did Abhay's phone show when the hostel lights went out?
qa.a: It showed six percent when the hostel lights died at nine.

qa.q: Why did Abhay keep waking his screen even though the battery was low?
qa.a: He was anxious and afraid of being turned down, so every minute without Nandini's reply felt huge and he could not stop checking.

qa.q: What could help Abhay at this uncertain stage, before he reads meaning into the next delay?
qa.a: He could remind himself that a slow reply usually means someone is busy, and put the phone away for a while instead of treating each gap as a verdict.

qa.q: How might Nandini see the invitation when she finally replies?
qa.a: Nandini seems pleased, even suggesting a time, and is probably unaware that her eleven minutes of silence felt enormous to Abhay.

grounding: Shows a young man who has started replying to stories and suggesting chai, with fear of rejection making reply speed feel huge.
